title: The Five Solids and the Ellipse: Kepler from Weil der Stadt to the Lost Grave at Regensburg
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Comet and the Red Moon: Weil der Stadt and Leonberg

stops.name: Weil der Stadt, the premature son
stops.date_confidence: attested; the hour of about half past two in the afternoon comes from Kepler's own retrospective horoscope of himself, not from a register. The date is transmitted in the Julian calendar, as standard biography gives it; the Gregorian equivalent would fall in January 1572.
stops.campa: In the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt, about half past two in the afternoon, Katharina Guldenmann bears a son to Heinrich Kepler, a mercenary who will drift in and out of the household for the short remainder of his attendance on it. The child comes early and comes weak, and will spend his life sick with something. Decades later he will cast his own nativity backward to this hour and this room, and set down the position of every planet over a house in Swabia on the afternoon of the twenty-seventh of December.
suggested_refs: The Kepler-Geburtshaus at Weil der Stadt, the birth house surviving as a museum
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Leonberg, the inn and the German school
stops.date_confidence: year attested by MacTutor; month and day set to 01 for ordering, the family's move being dated only to the year.
stops.campa: The family moves to Leonberg in the duchy of Württemberg, where Heinrich keeps an inn between campaigns and the boy is put through the German school and then the Latin. Württemberg runs a ladder for poor clever children: examination, scholarship, seminary, pulpit, and the duchy pays for the whole climb and expects a pastor at the top of it. Kepler is set on the first rung because there is no other rung his family could buy. His father leaves for the wars in the Low Countries and does not come back.
suggested_refs: The Latin school of Leonberg, first rung of the Württemberg scholarship system
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Leonberg, the great comet of 1577
stops.date_confidence: attested as a childhood memory Kepler himself recorded; the year is firm, the month is set from the known apparition of the Great Comet of 1577, and no source gives the day.
stops.campa: His mother takes him up onto high ground outside the town to look at the great comet standing over Swabia. He is about six. He will remember it the whole of his life and will write it down; it is one of the two things the sky hands him before he can construe Latin. All of Europe is reading the same object as a warning of war, of plague, of the death of princes. What the child keeps is the walk out of the town in the dark, and his mother stopping on the high ground and pointing.
suggested_refs: The Great Comet of 1577, observed across Europe and measured for parallax by Tycho Brahe from Hven

stops.name: Leonberg, the lunar eclipse of 1580
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01 for ordering. The attribution is corrected here: the Colegio dossier gave the father as the parent who called him outdoors, but both the German and English Wikipedia accounts give the mother for both childhood sky events.
stops.campa: Four years on she calls him outdoors again, and the moon goes into the earth's shadow and turns deep red over Württemberg. He is nine years old, and this is the second time she has taken him out of the house at night to look at something. He sets down both nights among the earliest things he can remember, the comet and the red moon, and both come from the same woman. Forty years from this evening the duchy of Württemberg will open a witchcraft file on her, and he will spend six years and more than nine hundred gulden fighting it.
suggested_refs: Kepler's own recollections of the 1577 comet and the 1580 eclipse, the two dated memories of his childhood

segments.name: The Scholarship Ladder: Adelberg, Maulbronn, Tübingen

stops.name: Adelberg, the lower seminary
stops.date_confidence: year attested by MacTutor; month and day set to 01 for ordering.
stops.campa: At thirteen he passes into the Protestant seminary at Adelberg, an old Premonstratensian abbey that the Reformation converted into a boarding school for boys the duchy intends to turn into pastors. The day is Latin, Greek, scripture, and prayer, run on a bell. The boys who survive Adelberg go on to Maulbronn, and from Maulbronn to Tübingen, and from Tübingen into parishes. Kepler is quick, quarrelsome, and disliked by the others, and he keeps a written record of his own faults.
suggested_refs: Adelberg Abbey, lower Protestant seminary of the Württemberg Klosterschule system
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Maulbronn, the higher seminary
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Britannica; month and day set to 01 for ordering.
stops.campa: Two years on he moves to Maulbronn, the great Cistercian house north of Stuttgart, where the cloister is intact, the timetable is monastic, and the boys sleep in the monks' old dormitory. He is distinguished, he is ill, and he is alone. The autobiographical notes he keeps set down the beatings, the fevers, and his own bad temper in the same flat hand he will later use on planetary positions. He is being trained to preach, and he expects a parish at the end of it.
suggested_refs: Maulbronn Monastery, higher seminary of the Württemberg system

stops.name: Tübingen, Mästlin teaching Copernicus in private
stops.date_confidence: matriculation attested to September 1589; day set to 01. The Magister Artium of 1591, folded into this stop, is attested to the year only.
stops.campa: He matriculates at the Tübinger Stift on a ducal scholarship to read theology, takes the Magister Artium in 1591, and stays on in the theology course expecting a parish at the end of it. Michael Mästlin holds the chair of mathematics. In the lecture hall Mästlin teaches Ptolemy, because Ptolemy is the curriculum; outside it, to the students he judges able, he explains the system of Copernicus, in which the earth is a planet and moves. Kepler takes the second lesson.
suggested_refs: The Tübinger Stift and Michael Mästlin's private Copernican teaching
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Tübingen, the disputation and the view from the moon
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dated c. 1593; month and day set to 01. The whole episode reaches us only through the tradition attached to the Somnium, and no source independent of that tradition was reachable.
stops.campa: As a student he defends the Copernican case in disputation and proposes, by the account that survives, an exercise describing the heavens as they would appear to an observer standing on the moon. The theologian Veit Müller is said to have refused it. Whether that lost exercise is the seed of the Somnium he will still be annotating thirty-six years later cannot be reconstructed from anything in the record. The only witness for the episode is the tradition that grew up around the Somnium itself.
suggested_refs: The Somnium tradition concerning a blocked student thesis on lunar perspective

segments.name: Graz: The Five Solids and the Edict

stops.name: Graz, the mathematics post he did not want
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1594; day set to 01.
stops.campa: Word comes from Graz that the Protestant Stiftsschule needs a mathematics teacher, and Württemberg puts forward Kepler, who has not finished his theology and wanted a pulpit. He goes because the duchy that paid for him has told him to go, and he goes reluctantly. He is twenty-two years old and teaching in a Catholic archduchy. In Inner Austria he is district mathematician as well as schoolmaster, which means calendars and prognostications for the province: weather, harvest, Turkish war.
suggested_refs: The Lutheran Stiftsschule of Graz and the office of provincial mathematician of Styria
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Graz, the figure on the classroom board
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, from Kepler's own account.
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of July, drawing a figure for his class, Kepler inscribes a circle in a triangle inscribed in a circle and sees the ratio between the two circles. Saturn and Jupiter. Plane figures fail him after that, so he goes to the solids, and of the perfect solids there are exactly five and no more, and there are exactly six planets, and five gaps between six spheres. Octahedron, icosahedron, dodecahedron, tetrahedron, cube. The number of the planets stops being an accident and becomes a proof.
suggested_refs: The nested-polyhedra model of the planetary spheres, conceived at Graz on 19 July 1595
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Graz, the Mysterium sent to Tübingen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01. The stop is pinned at Graz, where Kepler held his post and did the work; the printing was carried out at Tübingen under Mästlin's supervision.
stops.campa: The book goes to Mästlin at Tübingen, who sees it through the press. Mysterium Cosmographicum is the first substantial published defence of Copernicus by a working astronomer since Copernicus himself. The model in it is wrong. Nothing in the heavens is arranged around nested solids, and the man who will demonstrate that is its author. He never disowns it even so: in 1621 he reissues it half as long again, correcting himself in footnotes rather than withdrawing a line of the argument.
suggested_refs: Mysterium Cosmographicum (Tübingen, 1596) and its enlarged second edition of 1621
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Gössendorf, the miller's daughter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates are the municipality of Gössendorf to two decimals; German Wikipedia names Schloss Mühlegg as the residence but gives no coordinates for the castle itself.
stops.campa: He marries Barbara Müller von Mühleck, twice widowed and not yet twenty-four, daughter of the miller Jobst Müller, who objects at first that a schoolmaster is poor. The objection is negotiated away and the couple settle at Schloss Mühlegg in Gössendorf outside Graz. He is twenty-five years old, married into a mill, holding a Lutheran post in a province that will shortly expel its Lutherans in writing. Children are born to them here. Children are buried here.
suggested_refs: Schloss Mühlegg at Gössendorf, the Kepler residence 1597-1599

stops.name: Graz, the edict
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1598; day set to 01.
stops.campa: Archduke Ferdinand's Counter-Reformation edict orders every Protestant teacher and preacher out of Graz. The school closes and the clergy are given days to be gone. Kepler is expelled with the rest and then recalled, alone, because the province still wants its mathematician and its calendars. The exemption is a stay and not a pardon, and the city has already voted on what he is. He stays two more years and goes on producing the province's calendars.
suggested_refs: The Counter-Reformation edicts of Archduke Ferdinand in Inner Austria, 1598-1600

segments.name: Tycho's Numbers: Benátky and the Prague Court

stops.name: Benátky nad Jizerou, the data he came for
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: On the fourth of February Kepler reaches the castle at Benátky nad Jizerou, north-east of Prague, where Tycho Brahe has installed his instruments and twenty years of naked-eye observation, the most accurate positional record in the world. Tycho wants a calculator. Kepler wants the Mars observations, autonomy, and a salary, and neither man gets what he came for. Tycho releases the numbers in fragments; Kepler storms out and writes an apology. They work in the same house until Tycho dies.
stops.quote: I believe it was an act of Divine Providence that I arrived just at the time when Longomontanus was occupied with Mars. For Mars alone enables us to penetrate the secrets of astronomy which otherwise would remain forever hidden from us.
stops.quote_source: Kepler, Gesammelte Werke III, dedication of Astronomia Nova; quoted in James R. Voelkel, Johannes Kepler and the New Astronomy (Oxford, 1999), p. 66, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Benátky nad Jizerou castle, Tycho Brahe's Bohemian observatory
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Graz, the last departure
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Note that Kepler's February visit to Benátky preceded this departure: he returned to Graz in mid-1600 and was expelled for good in the autumn.
stops.campa: He comes back to Graz in the summer and is put to the choice in plain terms: convert, or go. On the thirtieth of September he goes, forfeiting salary, house, and the only secure post he has ever held, with a wife who does not want to leave her country, a stepdaughter, and no employment waiting at the far end. There is a scholar's version of this decision and there is the actual one, which is a cart on the autumn road to Bohemia with the household loaded on it. He is twenty-eight years old.
suggested_refs: The 1600 expulsion of the last Protestants from Graz

stops.name: Prague Castle, imperial mathematician
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier gave 24 October 1601, which is Tycho Brahe's death date; English Wikipedia states Kepler was appointed successor two days after Tycho's death, i.e. 26 October 1601.
stops.campa: Tycho Brahe dies on the twenty-fourth of October, and two days later Rudolf II appoints Kepler to succeed him as Imperial Mathematician. The court he now serves keeps astrologers, alchemists, and cabalists on retainer and expects its mathematician to cast horoscopes like the rest of them. The office also carries the Rudolphine Tables, promised to the emperor and unbuilt, and the observations required to build them, which Tycho's heirs claim at once as family property. Kepler has the papers in his hands. Whose they are is not settled for years.
suggested_refs: The disputed inheritance of Tycho Brahe's observational archive, Prague 1601-1604
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Prague, the astrology he means to reform
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day set to 01 for ordering within the segment. The relation to Pico is asserted in the corpus file for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola on the authority of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, and is a relation of text to text, not of persons.
stops.campa: The imperial mathematician is also the imperial astrologer, and Kepler does the work instead of pretending he does not. He publishes On the More Certain Foundations of Astrology, which throws out the houses, the decans, the whole inherited machinery, and keeps only the aspects, the angles between planets, on the argument that a soul seated in the earth responds to geometry. A century earlier Giovanni Pico della Mirandola had written the demolition of judicial astrology that nobody had answered. Kepler answers it from inside the practice, and goes on casting nativities for the emperor.
stops.quote: Discover the force of the heavens O Men: Once recognised it can be put to use: No use could be seen in unknown things.
stops.quote_source: De fundamentis astrologiae certioribus (1601), unknown translator, Opera Omnia vol. 1 (Heyder & Zimmer, 1858), pp. 417-438, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: De fundamentis astrologiae certioribus (Prague, 1601)
giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json, Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem
sources: giovanni_pico_della_mirandola.journey.json, citing the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

stops.name: Prague, the eye as an instrument
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01. Corrected as to place: MacTutor gives Frankfurt as the place of printing, but the work was written in Prague, where the stop is pinned.
stops.campa: Working on the question of why the moon measures as it does during an eclipse, Kepler writes the book that founds modern optics. In Ad Vitellionem paralipomena the eye stops being a philosophical puzzle and becomes a device: light enters the pupil, the lens refracts it, and an inverted image forms on the retina. What happens after the retina, he says, is a matter for the physicians and not for him. He also gets the inverse-square weakening of light with distance, the pinhole, and atmospheric refraction. It is printed at Frankfurt.
suggested_refs: Astronomiae pars optica / Ad Vitellionem paralipomena (Frankfurt, 1604)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Prague, the new star in the serpent-bearer
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1604; day set to 01. The stop folds in the publication of De stella nova in 1606, also attested to the year only.
stops.campa: In October a star appears in Ophiuchus that was not there before, brighter than Jupiter, and stays visible for a year. Kepler observes it, gathers the reports of other observers across Europe, and in 1606 publishes De stella nova in pede Serpentarii. The heavens above the moon are held to be incorruptible; here is a new thing standing in them, as there was a new thing in Cassiopeia in 1572, and the doctrine cannot survive both. Nobody watching in 1604 has any way of knowing it is the last such star this galaxy will show.
suggested_refs: SN 1604, the last supernova observed in the Milky Way
De stella nova in pede Serpentarii (Prague, 1606)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Prague, the war on Mars
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested; month and day set to 01. Printed at Heidelberg; the stop is pinned at Prague, where the work was done across the preceding years.
stops.campa: Six years of calculation on Tycho's Mars observations, done in ink by hand, and the circle will not close. A circular orbit with the sun off centre fits everything except eight minutes of arc, and Kepler will not throw away eight minutes of arc. He tries an oval, and then an ellipse with the sun at one focus, and the numbers come out. The planet also sweeps equal areas in equal times, running faster the nearer it is to the sun, which means the sky is no longer a diagram of motions but a problem with causes in it, and something in the sun is doing the pushing.
stops.quote: Gravity is a mutual affection between cognate bodies towards union or conjunction (similar in kind to the magnetic virtue), so that the earth attracts a stone much rather than the stone seeks the earth.
stops.quote_source: Astronomia Nova (1609), introduction; trans. Walter W. Bryant, Kepler (1920), ch. V (Wikiquote gives 'p. 35, f.')
suggested_refs: Astronomia nova (Heidelberg, 1609)
William H. Donahue's New Astronomy (Cambridge, 1992), the first complete English translation, 383 years after publication
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler
Walter W. Bryant, Kepler (1920), Project Gutenberg ebook 12406

stops.name: Prague, answering the Sidereus nuncius
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01. The stop folds in Dioptrice, published 1611, which the pool carries tagged R on the authority of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
stops.campa: Johannes Matthäus Wackher von Wackenfels, imperial councillor and friend, brings word to the door that Galileo Galilei has turned a telescope on the sky and found four moons going round Jupiter. Kepler owns no comparable instrument and cannot check a single observation. He answers within weeks anyway, in public, with the Dissertatio cum Nuncio sidereo, on the ground that the claims agree with the physics he already holds. The next year he publishes Dioptrice and works out the two-convex-lens telescope that inverts the image and carries his name.
suggested_refs: Dissertatio cum Nuncio sidereo (Prague, 1610)
Dioptrice (Prague, 1611) and the Keplerian telescope

stops.name: Prague, the death of Friedrich
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier bound this death to Barbara's under a single July date; German Wikipedia puts Friedrich's smallpox death in January 1611, roughly five months earlier. Day set to 01.
stops.campa: Smallpox takes his son Friedrich in January. The boy is six years old, and his father had drawn his nativity at birth. Five months from now the boy's mother will follow him. In the same winter Rudolf's brother Matthias marches troops into Prague and the emperor's authority comes apart street by street, and the salary owed the imperial mathematician stops being a debt anyone in the castle can be found to answer for. Kepler stays at the table with a dead Dane's observations and goes on with the Tables.
suggested_refs: The 1611 Passau invasion and the collapse of Rudolf II's authority in Prague

stops.name: Prague, the death of Barbara
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and not resolved: English Wikipedia gives 3 July 1611, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy timeline gives 3 August 1611. The July date is used here for ordering only.
stops.campa: Barbara, worn out by fever and by the burying of children, dies in the summer, five months after Friedrich. Fourteen years of a marriage in which, on his own account, neither of them could reach the other, and he does not write about the end of it as a release. Kepler is thirty-nine and has two surviving children. The court that employs him is dissolving, the emperor has months to live, and nothing holds him in Prague now but the papers. He begins writing letters to every Protestant town in the empire that might have use for a mathematician.
suggested_refs: Kepler's correspondence of 1611 seeking a post outside Prague
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Prague, the emperor dies
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1612; day set to 01.
stops.campa: Rudolf II, deposed in everything but name by his brother, dies in January in the castle where he kept his collections. Matthias succeeds him and lets Kepler keep the title of Imperial Mathematician, which from now on is a title and not a salary, on condition that he take a provincial post elsewhere. The Rudolphine Tables, named for a dead emperor who will never see a page of them, are still fifteen years from the press. Twelve years in Prague close. He packs the observations, the instruments, and the manuscripts himself.
suggested_refs: The Kunstkammer of Rudolf II at Prague Castle, dispersed after 1612

segments.name: Linz: The Barrels, the Third Law, the Harmony

stops.name: Linz, the provincial mathematician
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier gave August 1612; German Wikipedia gives April 1612 for the move, MacTutor puts the acceptance in late 1611 and Stanford gives only the bare year. Spring 1612 is used, with the day set to 01. Coordinates are the canonical Linz pin already used in robert_fludd.journey.json.
stops.campa: He arrives in Linz in the spring as mathematician to the estates of Upper Austria, keeping the imperial title without the imperial pay. He did not choose the city and did not want the office. The work is surveying, mapping the province, teaching, and the calendar. On the calendar he holds an awkward line in public: the Gregorian reform is astronomically the better instrument and he says so, while refusing to take it on a pope's authority alone. Tycho's numbers are still unfinished on the table.
suggested_refs: Kepler's provincial mapping and calendar duties for the estates of Upper Austria

stops.name: Linz, the second marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: He draws up a list of eleven candidates and works through it with the self-mockery of a man who knows precisely how he looks doing this, then marries the fifth: Susanna Reuttinger, an orphan of no standing raised in a school for poor girls. His friends had preferred the fourth. He picks the wedding day out of the almanac, choosing the date of a lunar eclipse on the reasoning that the astronomer in him would be occupied elsewhere and the bridegroom could have the day to himself.
stops.quote: won me over with love, humble loyalty, economy of household, diligence, and the love she gave the stepchildren
stops.quote_source: Kepler on Susanna Reuttinger, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Johannes Kepler'; underlying letter edition not independently opened
suggested_refs: Kepler's written survey of eleven marriage candidates, 1611-1613

stops.name: Linz, the wine barrels
stops.date_confidence: year of publication attested by MacTutor; month and day set to 01. The origin story, that the problem came from a gauger's rod at his own wedding, is reported rather than documented.
stops.campa: A merchant gauges the wine casks at his wedding by thrusting a rod in diagonally through the bunghole, and Kepler, watching, cannot see why one diagonal should be allowed to measure a volume. He works at it for a year. Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum takes a barrel as a solid of revolution and slices it into indefinitely many indefinitely thin discs and adds them, which is not yet a method with a name. He also finds that the Austrian barrel is very near the optimal shape for the wood it uses. The coopers had arrived at it by custom, without a proof.
suggested_refs: Nova stereometria doliorum vinariorum (Linz, 1615), a precursor of the integral calculus
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Linz, the fifteenth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day, by Kepler's own account in Harmonice Mundi Book V, which also gives the failed first attempt of 8 March 1618.
stops.campa: He had the idea on the eighth of March, calculated it wrong, and threw it out as false. It comes back on the fifteenth of May and this time the arithmetic holds: the square of a planet's period stands to the square of another's as the cube of its mean distance stands to the cube of the other's. Seventeen years of Tycho's observations and twenty years of his own obsession with harmony meet in a single proportion. He writes that he believed at first he was dreaming, that he had assumed his conclusion among his premises. Then he checked it.
stops.quote: and if you want the exact moment in time, it was conceived mentally on 8th March in this year one thousand six hundred and eighteen, but submitted to calculation in an unlucky way, and therefore rejected as false, and finally returning on the 15th of May and adopting a new line of attack, stormed the darkness of my mind.
stops.quote_source: Harmonice Mundi, Book V, ch. 3 (1618/1619); trans. Aiton, Duncan and Field (1997), p. 411, seen quoted with named translation on MacTutor
suggested_refs: Harmonice Mundi Book V, chapter 3, the narrative of the third law's discovery
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Linz, Harmonices mundi and the quarrel with Robert Fludd
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01. Note that the discovery narrative in Book V dates itself to 1618 while the volume appears in 1619, which is why some sources date the book 1618.
stops.campa: Five books: the regular figures, the congruences, the origin of harmonic proportion in music, the metaphysics and astrology of proportion, and then astronomy, where the third law sits in chapter three as one consequence among many of a creation built on ratio. The planets sing, and the intervals between their fastest and slowest motions are real musical intervals. In an appendix he goes after Robert Fludd, whose cosmic monochord strings the universe on a symbolism that measures nothing. Fludd answers from Frankfurt in 1621. Kepler answers him again in 1622.
stops.quote: Geometry is one and eternal shining in the mind of God. That share in it accorded to humans is one of the reasons that humanity is the image of God.
stops.quote_source: Harmonices Mundi (1619); trans. Judith V. Field, quoted in Field, 'Astrology in Kepler's Cosmology', in Astrology, Science, and Society, ed. P. Curry (1987), p. 154, via Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Harmonices mundi libri V (Linz, 1619)
robert_fludd.journey.json, which dramatizes the Kepler-Fludd exchange from Fludd's side at Linz and Frankfurt
Fludd, Monochordon Mundi Symphoniacum (Frankfurt, 1621); Kepler, Apologia pro suo opere Harmonices Mundi (1622)
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Linz, the Epitome and the Index
stops.date_confidence: the Epitome appeared in installments across 1618-1621; the Index placement is given in the pool as 1619 on a bibliographic synthesis cross-checked against MacTutor's listing, and was not independently verified against a Roman decree. Month set to 06 to order it after the Harmonices within the same year.
stops.campa: The Epitome astronomiae Copernicanae comes out in installments across four years, a textbook in question and answer that does for every planet, and for the moons of Jupiter, and for the moon itself, what Astronomia nova did for Mars. It is the book that actually carries the three laws into other people's hands. Rome puts it on the Index of Prohibited Books. Kepler keeps writing it, from a Protestant province of a Catholic empire, and publishes the later parts after the ban.
suggested_refs: Epitome astronomiae Copernicanae, installments of 1618-1621, and its placement on the Index librorum prohibitorum
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler
Colegio dossier synthesis of the standard bibliographic record

segments.name: The Witch of Leonberg: His Mother's Trial

stops.name: Linz, the letter out of Leonberg
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month set to 06 for ordering after the Nova stereometria within 1615. The stop is pinned at Linz because that is where Kepler was; the accusation itself was made at Leonberg.
stops.campa: A glazier's wife in Leonberg named Ursula Reinbold, chronically ill, says the illness came out of a bitter drink that Katharina Kepler gave her. In Württemberg in 1615 that sentence is not gossip. It is the opening move of a capital process. Katharina is about sixty-eight, a widow and an herb-woman, sharp-tongued, and litigious enough to sue her accuser for slander, which turns out to be the worst available response. Her son holds an imperial title and no standing whatever in the duchy of his birth. The news reaches him in Linz in the course of the year.
suggested_refs: The Reinbold accusation of 1615 and the opening of the Leonberg proceedings

stops.name: Leonberg, taking his mother out
stops.date_confidence: attested to December 1616; day set to 01.
stops.campa: He comes back to Württemberg in December and gets his mother out, carrying her to Linz to live in his house while the case goes on building behind her. It does not stop building. He is the Imperial Mathematician, which is why the duchy takes the accusation seriously in the first place and why it will not quietly let the thing lapse. Six years of it: depositions, an accusation running to dozens of counts, and a ducal court that does not let go of a file once the file is open.
suggested_refs: The old Vogtei at Leonberg, the Stonehouse, where Katharina Kepler was held during the local phase of the proceedings

stops.name: Güglingen, the arrest and the son for counsel
stops.date_confidence: arrest attested to 7 August 1620. Coordinates for Güglingen are given to low precision in the source; the specific cell is not located. German Wikipedia's Güglingen article did not itself carry the detention when fetched, which reaches this file through the Leonberg article.
stops.campa: On the seventh of August they take her at Heumaden and cart her to Güglingen, where she is held under a guard whose wages her own family has to pay. She is about seventy-three. Kepler leaves Linz, leaves the Tables, and comes to conduct the defence himself, drafting the legal argument and submitting it under his own name: an imperial mathematician arguing points of evidence in a witchcraft file. The detention runs four hundred and five days. The costs pass nine hundred gulden.
suggested_refs: Kepler's written defence of his mother, submitted to the Württemberg court, 1620-1621

stops.name: Güglingen, the territio verbalis
stops.date_confidence: corrected. The dossier gave September 1621; both English and German Wikipedia date the court hearing and the threat of torture to 20 August 1621, with release following in October, about six weeks later rather than the following month.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of August she is brought before the executioner and the instruments are shown to her one at a time and described, each with an account of what it does to a body. The procedure has a name, territio verbalis, and is not counted in law as torture. The court has spent six years assembling its case, and without a confession there is nothing in that case a Württemberg court can carry to a sentence. She is told to confess. She does not confess.
suggested_refs: The territio verbalis of 20 August 1621 in the Württemberg criminal procedure

stops.name: Roßwälden, released and dead within six months
stops.date_confidence: death attested to 13 April 1622; the release is attested to October 1621, after roughly 405 days of pretrial detention.
stops.campa: She is let out in October, acquitted for want of a case, after four hundred and five days in a cell whose guard her family had to pay for. She dies at Roßwälden on the thirteenth of April, about seventy-four years old, six months after the door opened. The other women accused in Württemberg in those years had no son at the imperial court with the time, the money, and the legal Latin to fight a file for six years. Katharina Kepler was never convicted and never sentenced.
suggested_refs: The Württemberg witchcraft proceedings of 1615-1621 against Katharina Kepler, closed without conviction

stops.name: Linz, the fire in the printing quarter
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1626; day set to 01.
stops.campa: The peasants of Upper Austria rise against Bavarian occupation and forced re-Catholicization, and the rising closes on Linz. Kepler is inside the walls through the siege. Fire takes the quarter where the printing house stands and destroys the press and the type laid aside for the Rudolphine Tables. Twenty-five years of work is reduced to a manuscript in a man's own keeping, and the manuscript survives only because it is with him and not in the shop.
suggested_refs: The 1626 Upper Austrian Peasants' War and the siege of Linz

stops.name: Ulm, the move with the manuscript
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1626; day set to 01. Coordinates are the Ulm old town; the address of Jonas Saur's shop was not confirmed.
stops.campa: He gets permission to take the printing out of the province and goes to Ulm with the manuscript, the household, and the paper. The printer is Jonas Saur. Kepler is fifty-four, and he has been carrying the same book since he was twenty-nine and living in Prague in a house he shared with a man he could not get along with. He stands over the whole operation: the typography, the diagrams, the paper stock, the arithmetic of the financing. He pays for a great deal of it out of his own pocket.
suggested_refs: Jonas Saur's printing house at Ulm, 1626-1627

stops.name: Ulm, the Tables printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1627; day set to 01.
stops.campa: The Tabulae Rudolphinae come off the press in September in an edition of a thousand copies: Tycho's star catalogue, Kepler's elliptical theory, and logarithms, giving planetary positions at an accuracy no earlier table approached. Navigators will use them. Astronomers will use them for a century. The work has taken twenty-six years, and it has outlived the emperor it is named for and the astronomer whose observations fill it. The frontispiece is a temple of astronomy held up by the men who came before him, and Kepler put himself in a small panel of the base, at a desk.
suggested_refs: Tabulae Rudolphinae (Ulm, 1627) and its allegorical frontispiece

stops.name: Prague, presenting the Tables and asking for the money
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01. Corrected as to figures: the dossier placed the ~12,000 gulden arrears here, but that is the sum standing at Kepler's death in 1630. The printing-period figure is 6,299 florins owed by the Imperial Court, of which he recovered 2,000.
stops.campa: He carries presentation copies of the finished Tables back to Prague and puts them into the hands that owe him money. On the printing alone the Imperial Court stood at six thousand two hundred and ninety-nine florins; he recovers two thousand and pays the rest himself. He is fifty-six and known across Europe, and he is looking for a patron. The larger account, three decades of unpaid imperial salary, is not settled here, and it is not settled anywhere afterwards either.
suggested_refs: The imperial arrears owed to Kepler, unsettled from 1601 to his death

stops.name: Żagań, under Wallenstein
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day.
stops.campa: Albrecht von Wallenstein, generalissimo of the imperial armies and newly made Duke of Sagan, offers Kepler a house, a press, and a salary, and on the twentieth of July Kepler moves his family into Silesia. Wallenstein wants horoscopes. The town speaks a language Kepler does not have, the promised facilities arrive slowly, and the pay arrives more slowly than that. He writes to Matthias Bernegger about the distance from any large city and the cost of getting a letter in and out of it.
stops.quote: It is loneliness which makes me oppressed here, far away from the large cities, and letters come and go only slowly, and are causing great expense.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Matthias Bernegger, March 1629, quoted in English Wikipedia, 'Johannes Kepler'; underlying letter edition not independently opened
suggested_refs: Wallenstein's ducal court at Sagan and its patronage of Kepler, 1628-1630

stops.name: Żagań, the press and the notes to the dream
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day set to 01. Corrected as to relationship: Jacob Bartsch was Kepler's collaborator in 1629 and became his son-in-law only in March 1630, so the dossier's 'son-in-law' at this date is an anachronism.
stops.campa: He sets up a press at Sagan with Jacob Bartsch, his astronomical collaborator and, from March 1630, his son-in-law, and prints ephemerides. In the same rooms he keeps adding to the Somnium, the dream in which a boy is carried to the moon by a daemon and looks back at an earth that turns: the only place he ever wrote out what Copernican astronomy looks like from a standpoint that is not the earth. The notes he has hung on it now run past two hundred and are longer than the dream.
suggested_refs: Somnium, seu opus posthumum de astronomia lunari, printed at Frankfurt in 1634 by Ludwig Kepler with Jacob Bartsch's assistance
Edward Rosen's translation, Kepler's Somnium (Wisconsin, 1967; Dover, 2003)

stops.name: Regensburg, the last ride
stops.date_confidence: given in the Stanford Encyclopedia timeline and corroborated by standard chronology; carried in the pool tagged R rather than A.
stops.campa: On the eighth of October he leaves Sagan on horseback for Regensburg, where the imperial diet is sitting and where the officers of the treasury can be reached in person. The arrears stand near twelve thousand gulden. He is fifty-eight, he has been on the road for most of thirty years, and it is autumn in the middle of the Thirty Years' War. He rides it. Susanna and the children stay behind in Silesia. He is on the road the better part of a month and arrives in Regensburg in November, ill.
suggested_refs: The imperial diet at Regensburg, 1630, and Kepler's outstanding salary claim
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Regensburg, the fever
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Coordinates are those of the Keplergedächtnishaus given by German Wikipedia, 49 degrees 1 minute 16 seconds north, 12 degrees 5 minutes 37.7 seconds east; the identification of the house as the death house rests on that article.
stops.campa: He takes lodgings in a house on the street that will later be renamed for him and does not get up again. The fever is short. The physicians of Regensburg arrive at no diagnosis, and later ages have proposed several without agreeing on one. He dies on the fifteenth of November, aged fifty-eight, with the salary unpaid, the Somnium unprinted, and his family four hundred miles away in Silesia. The house is still standing. It was rescued from demolition in 1959 and opened as a museum two years later.
suggested_refs: The Keplergedächtnishaus at Regensburg, opened as a museum in 1961
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler

stops.name: Regensburg, the grave that was taken apart
stops.date_confidence: burial attested to 19 November 1630 at the Petersfriedhof. Coordinates are a Regensburg city-centre placeholder: the Petersfriedhof lay outside the walls to the south-west and its exact site is not recoverable, which is the point of the stop. German Wikipedia dates the razing to 1632-1633 rather than to a specific month.
stops.campa: He is buried on the nineteenth of November in the Petersfriedhof, the Protestant cemetery outside the walls. Within three years the war reaches the ground itself: troops pull the cemetery apart to raise artillery positions, and the grave goes with it. Nothing marks where he lies, because there is no longer a where. Regensburg will raise him a monument in 1808 near where the grave was thought to have been, and will move it west when the railway station is built. The epitaph he had written for himself survives only because a later hand copied it down off a stone that no longer exists.
stops.quote: Mensus eram coelos, nunc terrae metior umbras; Mens coelestis erat, corporis umbra iacet.
stops.quote_source: Kepler's self-composed epitaph, transmitted through the Regensburg antiquarians Georg Serpilius and Johann Philipp Ostertag; de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Kepler
suggested_refs: The lost Petersfriedhof at Regensburg
The Kepler monument at Regensburg by Emanuel d'Herigoyen, 1806-1808, moved west when the railway station was built in the 1890s
The bronze monument by August von Kreling on the Marktplatz of Weil der Stadt, unveiled 1870
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews, biography of Kepler
